title: Terraform Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Terraform lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Configuration before action
entries.summary: Infrastructure as code means describing resources in files. Terraform reads those files and compares the desired result with recorded state.
notes: A tool that can manage infrastructure must be pointed at the intended project.

entries.name: A local resource example
entries.summary: terraform_data is a built-in resource that stores an input in Terraform state. It does not create a cloud machine.
notes: Do not add provisioner commands to this simple practice resource.

entries.name: Initialise the folder
entries.summary: init prepares a working directory. Backend configuration controls where state is stored; this practice keeps remote backends disabled.
notes: init does not mean a configuration is safe to apply.

entries.name: Format and validate
entries.summary: fmt checks or rewrites formatting. validate checks whether the configuration is internally valid after needed initialization.
notes: Validation does not prove the planned infrastructure is appropriate or affordable.

entries.name: Variables accept inputs
entries.summary: A variable declares an input and can provide a default. Types make the expected kind of value clear.
notes: A variable default is not a safe place for a real secret.

entries.name: Outputs show selected values
entries.summary: An output exposes a useful result from the configuration. It does not automatically make a private value safe to publish.
notes: Marking an output sensitive hides some display, but does not remove it from state.

entries.name: Read a plan
entries.summary: plan describes proposed changes. It gives you a chance to review before choosing whether to apply.
notes: Do not approve a plan you have not read, especially one that removes resources.

entries.name: State records managed resources
entries.summary: State links configuration to managed objects and their data. It can contain sensitive information, so treat it as important private project data.

example.code:
Configuration: what you want
State: what Terraform recorded
Provider reads: what exists now

notes: Do not edit state files manually as a normal way to change resources.

entries.name: Local values name expressions
entries.summary: locals name calculated values used inside a configuration. They are not inputs supplied from outside like variables.
notes: Use local.greeting for a local value and var.club_name for a variable.

entries.name: References express dependencies
entries.summary: A reference to another resource's result tells Terraform about a dependency. It can then choose a valid order of work.
notes: File order alone is not how Terraform decides resource dependencies.

entries.name: Modules package configuration
entries.summary: A module is a group of Terraform configuration files used together. The current folder is the root module; other modules can be called from it.

example.code:
Root module
  -> local module for a repeated group of settings
Module inputs: variables
Module results: outputs

notes: Do not trust a downloaded module without reading what it manages.

entries.name: Separate review from applying
entries.summary: apply performs the reviewed changes. A safe workflow checks scope, target and the exact plan before changing any real resources.

example.code:
Read configuration
Check working directory and state target
Validate and plan
Review proposed effects
Apply only when authorised

notes: Never run broad destruction commands against a project you do not fully own and understand.
